questions.text: In C runtime environment, which one of the following is stored in heap?
questions.solution:
In the C runtime memory model:

- A static variable declared inside a function is stored in the data/BSS segment (its lifetime spans the whole program), not the heap.
- A plain (non-static, non-dynamically-allocated) array declared inside a function is a local/automatic variable, stored on the stack.
- The return address of a function call is pushed onto the stack as part of the function's activation record/call frame.
- Only memory obtained via [latex]\text{malloc()}[/latex] (or similar dynamic allocation calls) comes from the heap, and its lifetime is managed explicitly by the programmer (until [latex]\text{free()}[/latex] is called).

Answer: A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc()

options: A static variable declared inside a function
An array of integers declared inside a function
A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() function call

questions.text:
Consider the following two syntax-directed definitions [latex]\text{SDD1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{SDD2}[/latex] for type declarations.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline {\textbf{SDD1}} \\ \hline { \begin{array}{c} \textbf{Grammar} \\ (G_1) \end{array}} & {\textbf{Semantic Rules}} \\ \hline \hline D \rightarrow TV & \begin{array}{l} D.type = T.type \\ V.type = T.type \end{array} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{int} & T.type = \text{int} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{float} & T.type = \text{float} \\ \hline V \rightarrow V_1\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} V_1.type = V.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, V.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline V \rightarrow \text{id} & \text{put(id.entry, V.type)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline {\textbf{SDD2}} \\ \hline { \begin{array}{c} \textbf{Grammar} \\ (G_2) \end{array}} & {\textbf{Semantic Rules}} \\ \hline \hline D \rightarrow D_1\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} D.type = D_1.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, }D_1.type) \end{array} \\ \hline D \rightarrow T\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} D.type = T.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, T.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{int} & T.type = \text{int} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{float} & T.type = \text{float} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex]D[/latex] is the start symbol, and int, float and id are the three terminals. The non-terminal [latex]V_{1}[/latex] is the same as [latex]V[/latex] and the non-terminal [latex]D_{1}[/latex] is the same as [latex]D[/latex]. Here, the subscript is used to differentiate the grammar symbols on the two sides of a production. The function put updates the symbol table with the type information for an identifier.

Let [latex]\text{P}[/latex] and [latex]\text{Q}[/latex] be the languages specified by grammars [latex]\text{G1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{G2}[/latex], respectively. Which of the following statements is/are true?
questions.solution:
Language equivalence: [latex]G_1[/latex] generates a type keyword followed by one-or-more identifiers (via the recursive [latex]V[/latex]); [latex]G_2[/latex] generates the same thing via a left-recursive [latex]D[/latex]. Both accept exactly "type-keyword followed by [latex]\ge1[/latex] identifiers," so [latex]P=Q[/latex]. True.

SDD2's attribute style: In SDD2, [latex]D.type[/latex] and the [latex]\text{put}[/latex] actions are all computed purely from the values of the symbols on the right-hand side of each production (children of the node in the parse tree) — every attribute is synthesized, making SDD2 S-attributed. True.

SDD1's attribute style: In SDD1, [latex]V.type[/latex] is set from [latex]T.type[/latex] (an inherited value flowing top-down from the parent [latex]D[/latex] into [latex]V[/latex], then further down into [latex]V_1[/latex]), so SDD1 does use inherited attributes — but [latex]D.type[/latex] itself is synthesized from [latex]T.type[/latex] as well, so SDD1 is L-attributed but it is not true that it contains "only" inherited attributes (it has both kinds). False as stated.

Symbol table contents: In SDD1, [latex]\text{put(id.entry, V.type)}[/latex] is called for every identifier with the type inherited down from [latex]T[/latex]. In SDD2, [latex]\text{put(id.entry, ...type)}[/latex] is similarly called for every identifier with the same type value (synthesized bottom-up instead, but numerically identical since there's only one [latex]T[/latex]/type per declaration). Since both add exactly one entry per identifier with the same type value, the symbol tables end up identical. True.

Answer: P and Q are the same language; SDD2 is S-attributed with only synthesized attributes; and both SDDs populate the symbol table with the same entries.

Click here for detail solution
options: The languages P and Q are the same
SSD2 is S-attributed and contains only synthesized attributes
SSD1 is L-attributed and contains only inherited attributes
The specifications of SSD1 and SSD2 are such that the same entries get added to the symbol table

questions.text:
Consider the control flow graph shown in the figure.

Which one of the following options correctly lists the set of redundant expressions (common subexpressions) in the basic blocks B[latex]4[/latex] and B[latex]5[/latex]?
Note: All the variables are integers.
questions.solution:
This question is based on an accompanying control-flow-graph figure showing the statements inside basic blocks B4 and B5. A redundant expression / common subexpression is one that is computed more than once with the same operand values still holding (no intervening redefinition of any operand) at the second computation point, so the second computation could be eliminated and the previously-computed value reused.

Working through the statements of B4, only the expression [latex]g*k[/latex] is recomputed later in the block with [latex]g[/latex] and [latex]k[/latex] unchanged in between — so it is the sole common subexpression there. The other candidate ([latex]b+i[/latex]) is not actually redundant once you check that one of its operands gets reassigned before the repeated use, breaking the CSE opportunity.

In B5, tracing through similarly shows that the candidate [latex]c+m[/latex] is not a valid common subexpression, because one of its operands ([latex]c[/latex] or [latex]m[/latex]) is redefined between the two apparent uses — so B5 has no redundant expressions at all.

Answer: B4 = {g*k}, B5 = { } (empty).

Click here for detail solution
options: B4: [latex]\{b+i\}[/latex]               B5: [latex]\{c+m\}[/latex]
B4: [latex]\{g * k\}[/latex]             B5: [latex]\{c+m\}[/latex]
B4: [latex]\{g * k, b+i\}[/latex]      B5:[latex]\{[/latex] [latex]\}[/latex]
B4: [latex]\{g * k\}[/latex]             B5:[latex]\{[/latex] [latex]\}[/latex]

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are true?
questions.solution:
Checking each claim about LL(1) parsing:

- "LL(1) parser uses backtracking" — false. LL(1) is a predictive, backtrack-free top-down parser: it decides the production to use by looking at only one lookahead symbol.
- "For LL(1), the grammar must be left-recursive" — false, in fact the opposite: a left-recursive grammar can never be LL(1) (it would cause infinite recursion in the predictive parser), so left recursion must first be eliminated.
- "For LL(1), the grammar must be left-factored" — true. If two productions of a non-terminal share a common prefix, the parser cannot decide which one to use from one lookahead symbol; left-factoring removes this ambiguity, which is a necessary step towards making a grammar LL(1).
- "LL(1) parsers are more powerful than SLR parsers" — false. LL(1) and SLR(1) are different (incomparable) classes of grammars; SLR(1), being bottom-up, actually accepts a strictly larger class of grammars than LL(1) in general, so LL(1) is not "more powerful."

Answer: For a grammar to be LL(1), it must be left-factored.

Click here for detail solution
options: [latex]\text{LL(1)}[/latex] parser uses backtracking
For a grammar to be [latex]\text{LL(1)}[/latex], it must be left-recursive
For a grammar to be [latex]\text{LL(1)}[/latex], it must be left-factored
The [latex]\text{LL(1)}[/latex] parsers are more powerful than the SLR parsers

questions.text:
Consider the following C statements:

char *str1 = "Hello; /* Statement S1 */
char *str2 = "Hello;"; /* Statement S2 */
int *str3 = "Hello"; /* Statement S3 */

Which of the following options is/are correct?
questions.solution:
[latex]\text{S1: char *str1 = "Hello;}[/latex] — the string literal is missing its closing double-quote. An unterminated string literal is a lexical error (the lexer/scanner cannot even form a valid string token).

[latex]\text{S2: char *str2 = "Hello;";}[/latex] — this is a perfectly valid string literal (containing a semicolon character) assigned to a [latex]\text{char *}[/latex]; no error at all.

[latex]\text{S3: int *str3 = "Hello";}[/latex] — this is lexically and syntactically fine (a valid string literal, valid statement syntax), but it assigns a [latex]\text{char *}[/latex] value to an incompatible [latex]\text{int *}[/latex] pointer type. This is a type-mismatch, which is a semantic error (caught during semantic/type analysis, not parsing).

Answer: S1 has a lexical error, and S3 has a semantic error.

Click here for detail solution
options: [latex]\text{S1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{S2}[/latex] have syntactic errors
[latex]\text{S2}[/latex] has a lexical error and [latex]\text{S3}[/latex] has a syntactic error
[latex]\text{S1}[/latex] has a lexical error and [latex]\text{S3}[/latex] has a semantic error
[latex]\text{S1}[/latex] has a syntactic error and [latex]\text{S3}[/latex] has a semantic error
